data.sourceWord: MCQ: Which of the following is NOT one of the four aims of human life for Hindus?
data.targetWord: Saguna

examples.en-GB: Answer: Saguna | Distractors: Artha; Dharma; Kama

data.sourceWord: Respect — speaking kindly and not discriminating
data.targetWord: Hindus show the personal virtue of respect by speaking kindly, not using offensive language, and not discriminating against others — honouring the divine present in all people.

examples.en-GB: AQA Q1.2 — ways Hindus show respect

data.sourceWord: Respect — towards teachers, elders and deities
data.targetWord: Hindus demonstrate respect by treating teachers, gurus and the elderly with honour, showing compassion, respecting the environment, and performing acts of worship such as darshan.

examples.en-GB: AQA Q1.2 — ways Hindus show respect

data.sourceWord: Tri-murti influence — understanding Brahman
data.targetWord: Belief in the Tri-murti (Brahma, Vishnu, Shiva) influences Hindus to study scripture and learn from gurus, understanding these three as manifestations of Brahman to attain moksha.

data.sourceWord: Tri-murti influence — focused devotion and pilgrimage
data.targetWord: Many Hindus focus devotion on one member of the Tri-murti; Shaivites worship Shiva and may make pilgrimage to Mt Kailash, while Vaishnavites worship Vishnu and may visit Vrindavan.

data.sourceWord: Karma — law of cause and effect
data.targetWord: The law of karma states that every action (thought, word and deed) has a consequence. Good actions (punya) bring joy and merit; harmful actions (papa) bring suffering and negative karmic debt.

data.sourceWord: Karma — link to samsara and moksha
data.targetWord: Karma is the reason humans continue to be reborn in samsara. The central aim of Hinduism is moksha — release from samsara — achieved by building karma positively through the four yogas.

data.sourceWord: Scripture: karma in the Mahabharata
data.targetWord: 'These actions which cause hurt and suffering to any other living beings are papa (sin); and punya (virtue) is those actions which bring joy and happiness to others.' (Mahabharata)

data.sourceWord: FOR: Avatars prove the absolute goodness of the divine
data.targetWord: 'For the protection of the good, and for the destruction of the wicked, for the establishment of Dharma, I am born from age to age.' (Bhagavad Gita) — avatars exist for the highest reasons, making belief in them foundational.

data.sourceWord: FOR: Belief in avatars leads to bhakti and moksha
data.targetWord: Belief in avatars inspires bhakti yoga (devotion), one of the paths to moksha. ISKCON is devoted entirely to the avatar Krishna; the belief directly enables the central aim of Hindu life.

data.sourceWord: AGAINST: Belief in Brahman is more fundamental
data.targetWord: Fully realising that Brahman is everything (Upanishads) is the ultimate aim for any Hindu — belief in avatars is merely a stepping stone to this deeper union with Ultimate Reality.

data.sourceWord: AGAINST: Avatars are a Vaishnavite concept only
data.targetWord: Belief in avatars is specifically a Vaishnavite concept. For Shaivites, who worship Shiva as Supreme Lord, avatars are not important — so the belief cannot be the most important for all Hindus.

data.sourceWord: MCQ: Which of the following refers to a statue of a deity?
data.targetWord: Murti

examples.en-GB: Answer: Murti | Distractors: Mandir; Mantra; Moksha

data.sourceWord: Land and rivers — sacred because everything is Brahman
data.targetWord: Hindus use land, hills and rivers for worship because everything is Brahman (Ultimate Reality). Rivers give life, are linked to deities (the Ganges to Shiva), and are venues for acts of worship.

examples.en-GB: AQA Q2.2 — why Hindus use land and rivers for worship

data.sourceWord: Rivers for ritual — cremation and rebirth
data.targetWord: Rivers such as the Ganges are used for cremation at the ghats in Varanasi, scattering ashes to aid and quicken rebirth. River water is also used in acts of Hindu worship.

examples.en-GB: AQA Q2.2 — why Hindus use land and rivers for worship

data.sourceWord: Hindu charities — education and employment for women
data.targetWord: Hindu charities support women's rights by educating orphaned girls (Commit2Change), creating jobs (Women on Wings), and running skills programmes to help women escape the poverty cycle.

data.sourceWord: Hindu charities — safety and legal support for women
data.targetWord: Sayfty educates women on self-defence and supports legal action after rape; WASH United provides free sanitary products and reduces menstruation taboos, empowering women in communities.

data.sourceWord: Hindu pilgrimage — gaining positive karma and devotion
data.targetWord: Pilgrimage to sacred sites (like Varanasi, said to be the gateway to moksha) generates positive karma (punya) through each act of worship and demonstrates total surrender to the divine.

data.sourceWord: Hindu pilgrimage — seeking healing and guidance
data.targetWord: Pilgrims may seek healing by bathing in the Ganges, scatter a relative's ashes to aid rebirth, or seek guidance from sadhus and gurus found at sacred places like Kumbh Mela.

data.sourceWord: Scripture: pilgrimage in the Rig Veda
data.targetWord: 'Flower-like the heels of the wanderer, His body groweth fruitful: All his sins disappear, Slain by the toil of sacred journey.' (Rig Veda)

data.sourceWord: FOR: Holi celebrates devotion and the triumph of good over evil
data.targetWord: The story of Prahlad's devotion to Vishnu saving him from Holika represents the power of faith. Symbolically, fire destroys the negativity within each person — directly linking to the path toward moksha.

data.sourceWord: AGAINST: Holi is a Vaishnavite festival — not universal
data.targetWord: Holi focuses on Vishnu saving Prahlad and Krishna, which may undermine its importance for Shaivites and Ganapatians who do not regard Vishnu as supreme. Diwali has a wider universal appeal.

data.title: The Concept of Brahman in Hinduism
data.sourceTitle: The Concept of Brahman in Hinduism
data.sourcePassage: Brahman is the Ultimate Reality in Hindu belief — the single divine source from which everything originates and to which everything returns. Brahman is infinite, eternal and beyond human comprehension. Because Brahman is so abstract, Hinduism teaches two ways of understanding the divine: Nirguna Brahman (without qualities, the impersonal absolute) and Saguna Brahman (with qualities, the personal god who can be worshipped in the form of the Tri-murti — Brahma the creator, Vishnu the preserver, and Shiva the destroyer). Many Hindus focus their worship on one deity as a path to understanding Brahman. The central aim of human life is moksha — liberation from the cycle of birth and rebirth (samsara) and reunion with Brahman. This is achieved through the four yogas: karma yoga (service), bhakti yoga (devotion), jnana yoga (knowledge), and raja yoga (meditation). The law of karma governs rebirth: good actions (punya) lead toward moksha while bad actions (papa) prolong samsara.
